title: 🎙️ Repair Culture & Practical Tech
description: Today is about things you can fix, keep running, and pass on — repair culture, right-to-repair wins and setbacks, gear that outlives its manufacturer's support window, and the maker ethos of building to last rather than building to replace. We're interested in tools, devices, and projects where longevity, repairability, and self-sufficiency intersect, especially in rural and off-grid contexts where you can't just run to a repair shop. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Repair Culture & Practical Tech' — the right to repair movement, gear that outlasts its manufacturer, DIY fixes, and tools built for longevity.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical conflict; natural disasters without an engineering or preparedness angle; wildlife and conservation; working-lands policy; Indigenous governance; science discoveries with no DIY or hardware relevance; financial market news.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Hands-on hardware journalism counts fully even without an explicit right-to-repair hook.
- 80-100: Directly about repairability — right-to-repair legislation wins and losses, iFixit-style teardowns scoring repairability, gear designed for user serviceability, products outliving manufacturer support and how owners keep them running, permacomputing, vintage hardware still in active use, open-source hardware, Rossmann-style repair advocacy, 3D-printed replacement parts, battery replacement guides, rural and off-grid repair self-sufficiency.
- 55-79: Hands-on maker and DIY content — builds, modifications, hardware hacks, workshop projects, practical electronics guides with real technical depth, 3D printing hardware and filament, off-grid and solar gear, home lab hardware, tools and workshop equipment, battery and power tech. Most genuine hands-on hardware journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Gadget and device reviews with some technical substance; consumer electronics touching software longevity or ecosystem lock-in; hardware whose selling point is open firmware or modular design.
- 10-29: Surface-level product announcements, gadget speculation, leaked specs, general tech news with no hardware or repair angle.

ANCHORS: 'Framework Laptop 16 teardown: a 9/10 repairability score' → 98. 'Oregon's right-to-repair law takes effect' → 92. 'Building a solar-powered Raspberry Pi weather station' → 68. 'Samsung teases thinner bezels on next Galaxy' → 15.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

This is an interesting take. Philippa Hardman explains the 'disappearance' of entry-level roles in learning and development as a consequence of the way AI is replacing human work at those lower levels. Nothing new there. But then comes the observation, "L&D work is going from a craft you learned by doing - producing courses, mastering tools, making things - to a discipline you're trusted to exercise: diagnosing problems, specifying solutions, judging quality and measuring impact." I wonder whether this is true - the professions I can think of, such as engineering, medicine and law, all depend a lot on developing through experience the sort of intuition and socialization needed to be 'professional'. Learning, in other words, by doing.

items.title: [Fast Company] How ‘Star Trek’ helped invent the future
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Star Trek first beamed into our lives at 8:30 p.m. on Sept. 8, 1966, and the science fiction world was never the same. The show, though canceled after just three seasons, went on to become a lasting pop culture phenomenon that has spawned an entertainment empire, with movies, spinoffs, merchandise, and a fan following that few intellectual properties can match.

But Star Trek proved to be more than just an entertainment property. The technology the show imagined inspired many future developers to try to recreate the gadgets they saw growing up. And some of those fantastical devices have become part of daily life, even if we’re still a long way from launching our own five-year mission to explore strange new worlds.

Here’s some of the on-screen technology that has become real.

Communicators

Captain Kirk and crew stayed in touch with each other and the Enterprise via a handheld device that flipped open. Modern technology managed to replicate that by 1989, with the release of the first Motorola StarTAC phone, and arguably perfected it with the Razr in 2004.

The technology, of course, has continued to improve, and the “communicators” we carry today, in the form of iPhones and the wide assortment of Android devices, do a lot more than just let us talk to others. Still, Martin Cooper, who has been credited with the invention of the first handheld cellular phone in the 1970s, said his inspiration for the first cell phone was, in fact, Star Trek‘s communicator.

Universal translators

Lt. Uhura had lots of duties on board the Enterprise, but figuring out what the aliens were saying wasn’t always one of them. That was the job of the ship’s universal translator. Today, there are several tools that provide instant translation of foreign languages, though they’re not too useful should a Gorn want to strike up a conversation.

Those range from apps such as Google Translate and iTranslate to AI-assisted earbuds like the Samsung Galaxy Buds4 line and Timekettle’s W4 Pro, as well as handheld translators like the Vasco V4 Language Translator Device.

Voice-interface computers

In 1966, seeing Mr. Spock talk with the ship’s computer was something few people could imagine. Today, millions of people do that on a regular basis, interacting with the Amazon Echo device sitting on their counter, asking Siri to call up some information, or even telling their vacuum to tidy up the floors. Most states, in fact, require drivers to avoid picking up their cell phones while behind the wheel but are just fine with voice interactions.

Medical tricorders

Dr. McCoy isn’t the only person with a tricorder medical scanner, though his is still much better than anything we have at the moment. A decade ago, a company called Scanadu showed off a handheld device that measured five vital signs in roughly 30 seconds. That company was acquired six years ago by Israeli healthcare startup Healthy.io.

Today’s smartwatches, meanwhile, fill some of the same roles as a tricorder, monitoring your heart rate, sleep schedule, blood pressure, and more.

Replicators

The advent of 3D printers has given us the ability to summon devices from thin air, much like viewers have seen in subsequent Star Trek shows (though it sometimes takes a day or two for them to assemble). The technology can create everything from custom prosthetics to engine parts to rocket engines, as used on the Aeon 1 rocket in 2023.

3D-printed food as it was presented on the show isn’t possible, but specialized devices can create edible layers using food powders and a liquid binder. That can make a decent confection, but it’s still a long way from learning to make Gagh.

Hyposprays

Shots on Star Trek were needle-free, something any child watching was particularly envious of. What few realized, though, was that jet injectors were actually already a thing at the time. The device uses high-pressure gas to propel a high-velocity stream of liquid medication through the skin. The tech is still around today, but doctors haven’t given up the needle for the most part. Sorry, kids.

(Coming soon?) Warp drive

OK, no, the warp drive is still a fantasy. Faster-than-light travel, as NASA will tell anyone who asks, is still imaginary at present. That doesn’t mean it has given up on the idea. NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, Ohio, houses the Breakthrough Propulsion Physics Project, where NASA engineers are hoping to produce “near-term, credible, and measurable progress toward the technology breakthroughs needed to revolutionize space travel and enable interstellar voyages.” The Tau Zero Foundation, meanwhile, is also seeking advances in propulsion that could make interstellar flight possible.

items.title: [Fast Company] The ‘Great Flattening’ rolls on as Uber lays off middle managers
items.content_html:
🔧 ✏️

Uber is reducing its workforce by 10%, or about 3,300 workers, in its largest job cuts since the pandemic, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi announced yesterday. 

The changes, which follow a period of solid growth at the ride-sharing giant, are intended to speed up decision-making by reducing the number of management layers, Khosrowshahi wrote in a memo to employees. The number of workers who sit seven or more layers from the CEO has fallen by 20%, and the number of “micro-teams” with only one or two reports has been cut nearly in half. 

The restructuring is further evidence that the so-called Great Flattening—the trend in the corporate world toward reducing layers of middle management—shows no signs of slowing down. In recent years, companies like Meta, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have aggressively eliminated managerial roles on the belief that, in the words of Mark Zuckerberg, “flatter is faster.” 

Spurred on by the rise of artificial intelligence, the Great Flattening has already reshaped the workforce dramatically. Overall, the average number of people reporting to managers has increased from 10.9 in 2024 to 12.1 in 2025 and is up nearly 50% since 2013, according to Gallup. In Korn Ferry’s “Workforce 2005: Power Shifts” survey, 41% of employees said their organization had reduced management layers. 

The Great Flattening has created a massive natural experiment in what happens when companies slim down middle management. Is there a point where “flatter” stops meaning “faster” and starts meaning “poorly managed”?

While the jury is still out, the results so far have been decidedly mixed. 

Several companies have touted productivity gains after engaging in aggressive “flattening” campaigns. The life science multinational Bayer, which trimmed as many as six organizational layers and reduced management positions by roughly two-thirds, has said that some product-development cycles have been dramatically shortened and that, overall, it is on track for €2 billion (around $2.3 billion) in annual organizational savings by the end of 2026.

At Citi, after an aggressive reorganization under CEO Jane Fraser reduced the number of management layers from 13 to eight, financial performance clearly improved. While it is impossible to attribute these gains directly to restructuring, it is safe to say that the management reductions didn’t cripple the company. 

However, other examples show that the Great Flattening could be taking a toll. After reducing its workforce by more than 20% in 2023, Meta saw jumps in revenue, operating income, and operating margin the following year—only to run into widespread employee discontent when it launched another restructuring earlier this year. 

Commentators have identified a number of long-term risks associated with cutting middle management too aggressively—from degrading institutional knowledge to sapping a key pipeline of future leaders—and floated novel solutions for manager burnout.

Indeed, for the middle managers who survive, the Great Flattening may be making a job that was already a pressure cooker completely intolerable. 

In January, 97% of managers surveyed told Gallup that they have some individual contributor responsibilities in addition to leading others. Managers who spent less than 40% of their time on individual contributor work reported higher engagement than those who spent more than 40%. Manager engagement has fallen 9 percentage points since 2022, including a 5-point drop (from 27% to 22%) between 2024 and 2025 alone. 

That may be the tension Uber is about to test. Khosrowshahi is betting that fewer layers and larger teams will make the company move faster. But as the Great Flattening enters its next phase, the more important question may be whether the managers left behind can keep up.
